Missoula property tax is billed by the offices named below.

Who bills what in Missoula

  • Montana Department of Revenue handles assessment.
  • Missoula County Clerk & Recorder/Treasurer bills and collects the tax.

Due dates

Real property taxes due on or before the last day in November and May (next business day if weekend/holiday); mail must be postmarked by due date. Delinquent: 2% penalty plus interest at 10% annualized; tax liens attach first business day in August.. See the official page.

Challenging your assessment

Request informal review with the Montana DOR via Form AB-26 within 30 days of the date on the classification and appraisal notice (late requests accepted until June 1, 2026 for TY2026 only), or appeal directly to the County Tax Appeal Board by filing with the county clerk and recorder within 30 days of the notice date (or within 30 days of the AB-26 determination). CTAB decisions may be appealed to the Montana Tax Appeal Board within 30 days, then district court (60 days). To preserve a refund, . See the official page.

Tax rate

We could not confirm the current Missoula rate on an opened page, so we do not state one.

Local notes

  • Montana structure: the state Department of Revenue appraises/classifies all real property; the county treasurer bills and collects (including city, school and special district levies). Cities do not assess or collect.
  • Appraisal cycle: residential/commercial valued every two years (2025-2026 cycle, valuation date January 1, 2024).
  • Delinquent taxes cannot be protested or appealed (Yellowstone County bill text).

Missoula by the numbers

The Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey counts about 75,600 people in Missoula, which makes it the 2nd largest of the 7 mt places we cover. The median value of an owner-occupied home is $427,400, 20% above the median of those 7 places. 48% of occupied homes are owner-occupied and 52% are rented, against a median of 60% owner-occupancy across the mt places. The median home was built in 1981, about 42 years ago, which matters for roofs, plumbing and inspection requests. These numbers describe Missoula as a whole, so a given street can sit well above or below them.

Where is Missoula and what does its layout mean for a house sale?

Missoula sits in western Montana, less than 25 miles from the Idaho border, at an elevation of 3,209 feet. The city covers about 35 square miles on a flat valley floor, with Mount Sentinel and Mount Jumbo rising steeply on its edges.

That flat floor is the old bed of Glacial Lake Missoula. The Clark Fork River enters through Hellgate Canyon, the Blackfoot River joins it about five miles east of downtown, and the Bitterroot River meets it on the western side. Missoula is often called the hub of five valleys, and houses range from older neighborhoods near the river to hillside lots on the slopes.

For a seller, the practical point is that the land around a Missoula house varies a lot. A river-bottom parcel, a lot on a steep slope and a house in a rural fire district outside city limits can all carry different tax bills and different buyer questions. Looking up the parcel before you list saves surprises later.

How did Missoula develop, and why does it still matter to sellers?

Missoula started as a trading post. Hell Gate Village was founded in 1860 to serve travelers on the Mullan Road, and the settlement moved to its present site in 1864 so a lumber and flour mill could use a better water supply. Missoula became the county seat in 1866, Fort Missoula was built in 1877, and the Northern Pacific Railway arrived in 1883.

The University of Montana opened in 1895. Timber carried the economy for a century, then the Bonner plywood plant closed in 2007, the Bonner sawmill in 2008 and the Smurfit-Stone pulp mill in 2010. The city has since leaned on education, health care and services.

The University of Montana is the largest employer, followed by Missoula County Public Schools and the two hospitals. The table below uses the figures in the city's 2023 Annual Comprehensive Financial Report, as summarized on Wikipedia.

Who bills Missoula property tax, and what is on the bill?

Missoula County collects the bill, even though many separate bodies set the rates. The County Clerk and Treasurer's office collects for every taxing jurisdiction in the county, so a single bill can include county, city, school, fire, transit and state university levies.

The county's 2026 tax-bill notice names the six largest jurisdictions likely to appear:

  • Missoula County Public Schools
  • City of Missoula
  • Missoula County
  • Missoula Urban Transportation District (Mountain Line)
  • Missoula Rural Fire District
  • Montana University System

Special districts for water, sewer, irrigation or bus service can add more lines. You can look up a bill at the county's property tax page, search by last name, address, geocode or taxpayer ID, and view a pie chart of how the bill splits among jurisdictions.

What are the 2026 and 2027 Missoula property tax dates?

The 2026 first-half payment must be postmarked by Monday, November 30, 2026, and the second half is due Tuesday, June 1, 2027. Both halves appear on one invoice, and no separate second-half bill is sent.

The county advises that if you mail a payment between November 26 and 30, you should hand it to a post office employee and ask for a counter postmark.

State law, MCA 15-16-102, sets half due by 5 p.m. on November 30 and half by 5 p.m. on May 31, and moves a weekend or holiday due date to the next business day. Primary residences can enroll in a seven-payment alternative schedule that runs from November 30 through May 31.

What happens if Missoula property tax goes unpaid before a sale?

Unpaid tax becomes a lien on the house, and the lien has to be cleared at closing. Taxes are delinquent after the date and time printed on the October or November bill. A 2% penalty applies, and interest runs at 10% annualized (5/6 of 1% a month under state law).

  • Late June or early July: delinquent notices are mailed.
  • First business day in August: the tax lien attaches, with a $75 tax lien certificate fee added to the property.
  • Late August: outside investors may buy the lien and take an assignment.
  • The county says a taxpayer has two to three years from the lien date to pay or risk losing the property.

If you plan to sell, ask the title company for a payoff figure that includes penalty and interest to the closing date. Delinquent tax is paid out of your proceeds, so a house with a lien can still sell, but your net shrinks.

How does the Montana tax rate change affect a Missoula house in 2026?

Montana's 2026 structure taxes a primary residence at a lower tiered rate than a second home. The Department of Revenue lists 0.76% on the first $378,000 of market value, 0.90% from $378,001 to $756,000, 1.10% from $756,001 to $1,511,999, and 1.90% above that.

A house that is not a primary residence or long-term rental falls under a flat 1.90%. The department names second homes, short-term rentals and vacant residential lots in that group. To qualify for the lower rate, an owner must live in the home seven or more months of the year, and long-term rentals must be rented for 28 or more days at a time for at least seven months.

This matters in Missoula for heirs and landlords. If you inherit a house and nobody lives there, or a tenant leaves and the unit sits empty, the lower rate may stop applying. The Department of Revenue explains enrollment and refunds on its 2026 property tax page.

How do you dispute a Missoula assessment?

The state, not the county or city, values your property, so a dispute starts with the Department of Revenue. The Montana Department of Revenue reappraises residential property every two years, and the Missoula County treasurer's page says to file an appeal as soon as you get your notice.

There are two routes. You can send a Request for Informal Classification and Appraisal Review (Form AB-26) to the department online, or you can appeal directly to the Missoula County Tax Appeal Board through the same online application at mtab.mt.gov/appealform.

Your property record card, which lists the buildings and characteristics the state used, is available online. Check it for errors before you file.

What do you file when a Missoula house is sold?

Every transfer of real property in Montana needs a Realty Transfer Certificate filed with the county clerk and recorder when the deed is presented for recording. The Montana Department of Revenue form warns that an inaccurate or missing certificate can bring a $500 penalty, six months in jail, or both.

The form asks for several things a seller should have ready:

  • The names and mailing addresses of seller and buyer, plus the last four digits of each Social Security number or federal ID number.
  • Whether the property was the seller's principal residence, defined as occupied for at least seven months.
  • The sale price and whether the financing was cash, FHA, VA or contract.
  • A water right disclosure signed by the seller.

The form also reminds sellers that any gain is Montana-source income and should be reported on a return. The department cross-checks the identification numbers against income tax filings. For water rights, if the house is on city water, you check the public-supply box. The Missoula office of the Department of Natural Resources and Conservation handles Granite, Mineral, Missoula and Ravalli counties.

What does Missoula's climate mean for a roof, heating and a sale?

Missoula has cold, moderately snowy winters and hot, dry summers. Winter snowfall averages about 39.5 inches, snow lies on the ground about 120 days a year, and the airport records about 45 days a year that never rise above freezing.

Summer is hot as well. There are about 24 days a year at or above 90 degrees, and the record high is 107 degrees, last reached on June 30, 2021. Those swings are hard on roofing, gutters, furnaces and exterior paint, and buyers' inspectors look for all of them.

If your house needs a roof or a furnace, a conventional sale can stall at the inspection stage. Selling as-is to a cash buyer removes the repair negotiation, though the price will reflect the condition.

More questions about Missoula, MT Property Tax Guide

What is Missoula property tax and who collects it?

Missoula property tax is a set of levies from the county, city, schools, fire, transit and the university system, all collected by the Missoula County Clerk and Treasurer. The Montana Department of Revenue sets the value, and the county bills it.

When is Missoula property tax due?

The first half of the 2026 bill must be postmarked by Monday, November 30, 2026, and the second half is due Tuesday, June 1, 2027. Check the county's property tax page, since dates move when a deadline falls on a weekend or holiday.

Can I sell a Missoula house with unpaid property tax?

Yes. The tax, penalty and interest are paid from your proceeds at closing, so the title company needs a current payoff amount. A lien that attached in August can be cleared the same way.

What penalty applies to late Missoula property tax?

The county lists a 2% penalty plus interest at 10% annualized. The county's delinquent tax page says the lien attaches on the first business day of August and adds a $75 tax lien certificate fee.

What form do I file when I sell a house in Missoula?

You file a Realty Transfer Certificate with the Missoula County Clerk and Recorder when the deed is recorded. It covers parties, price, financing, principal residence status and water rights.

How do I appeal my Missoula assessment?

File an AB-26 informal review request with the Department of Revenue, or appeal to the Missoula County Tax Appeal Board online. The county advises filing as soon as the notice arrives.

Does an empty inherited house in Missoula get the lower tax rate?

Not automatically. The state's lower tiered rate is for primary residences and qualifying long-term rentals, and the department lists second homes and vacant residential lots at a flat 1.90%.
